name: Insomnia
tagline: Desktop API client for firing HTTP, GraphQL and gRPC requests, with collections, environments and team sync.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The thing you actually use Insomnia for, sending an HTTP request with headers, auth and a body, then saving it into a folder with environment variables, is a one-session build. An agent can give you a local request runner with collections stored as JSON on disk, a proxy so CORS never bites, history, and curl import, and for a solo developer that is genuinely enough. The gaps show up at the edges: gRPC, WebSocket and SSE clients, OpenAPI import, code generation, a cookie jar, and the thousand small keyboard-and-layout decisions that make a mature client feel fast. The paid tiers are mostly cloud sync, RBAC and SSO, and if you are one person a git repo of JSON files replaces all of that. Also worth saying out loud: the free tier plus git already covers most solo use, so the honest reason to build is control, not cost.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that stores request collections and environments as JSON files on disk and fires them through a local proxy so you can inspect the raw response.
requirements: A folder you are willing to commit to git if you want sync
Nothing else; no accounts, no cloud
whatYouLose: gRPC, WebSocket and SSE clients, plus streaming response viewers
OpenAPI and Postman collection import, and code generation in a dozen languages
The plugin ecosystem and community auth helpers, including full OAuth 2 flows with token refresh
Encrypted cloud sync, shared workspaces, RBAC and SSO for teams
Packaged desktop builds, auto updates, and the polish of keyboard-first navigation and response diffing
moatNotes: The moat is breadth of protocol support and years of small UX decisions, not data. Nobody is locked in by their request collection.
whyPeopleStillPay: Teams pay because request collections turn into shared institutional knowledge, and once that happens you want sync, access control and SSO rather than a git repo of JSON and a Slack thread about who broke the staging environment. Individuals mostly do not pay, and the free tier is a big part of why. The other reason is protocol breadth: the day you need gRPC reflection or a WebSocket session, your weekend build stops being cute and you reopen the real client.
notes: Building an API client is the developer equivalent of building a to-do app, which is exactly why an agent is good at it.
prompt:
Build a local-first HTTP API client called "Reqbox" that runs entirely on my machine.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20, TypeScript, Fastify for the backend.
- React + Vite for the frontend, plain CSS, no component library.
- No database. All state lives in ./workspace as human-readable JSON files.
- One command, `npm run dev`, starts the API on port 4000 and the UI on 5173 with a proxy.

Data model on disk:
- ./workspace/collections/NAME.json holds an ordered tree of folders and requests.
- A request has: name, method, url, headers array, query params array, auth (none | bearer | basic), body (none | json | form | raw), and notes.
- ./workspace/environments/NAME.json holds flat key/value pairs. One environment is active at a time, stored in ./workspace/state.json.
- Template syntax {{VAR}} in url, headers, params and body is substituted from the active environment at send time. Show the resolved request before sending.
- Secrets: any env value whose key ends in _SECRET is read from process.env instead of the file, loaded from .env. Ship a .env.example and gitignore .env.

Backend:
- POST /api/send takes a resolved request, performs it server-side with fetch so the browser never hits CORS, and returns status, headers, timing in ms, body size, and the raw body text.
- Append every send to ./workspace/history.jsonl, capped at the last 500 entries.
- CRUD endpoints for collections and environments that write files atomically.

Frontend:
- Three panes: collection tree on the left, request editor in the middle, response on the right.
- Response pane: pretty-printed JSON with collapsing, raw text toggle, headers tab, status and timing badge.
- Cmd+Enter sends. Cmd+S saves. Sidebar filter box.
- Import: paste a curl command and it becomes a request. Export: turn any request back into curl.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build: gRPC, WebSocket, SSE, GraphQL schema introspection, OAuth flows, plugins, accounts, telemetry, cloud sync, Electron packaging.

Deliverables: working code, a seeded example collection hitting httpbin.org, and a README with setup, the file layout, and the note that syncing means committing ./workspace to git.
